aliases.name: Onyare'kowa
aliases.region: Iroquois territory; 'great horned serpent' in oral tradition

description.summary: An aquatic cryptid said to inhabit Lake Champlain on the border of Vermont, New York, and Quebec. Reported as a long-necked, serpentine animal in the loch-monster mould, with several hundred reported sightings since the 19th century.
description.full: Champ is the popular name for a purported large aquatic cryptid said to inhabit Lake Champlain, a long, deep freshwater lake straddling the border of Vermont, New York, and the Canadian province of Quebec. Reports describe a serpentine or long-necked creature commonly compared with the Loch Ness Monster. Iroquois tradition records giant serpents in the lake — the Mohawk Onyare'kowa — long before European contact, and 19th-century newspaper reports describe sightings such as those of 'Captain Crum' (1819) and Sheriff Nathan Mooney (1883). The most famous modern piece of evidence is the 1977 photograph by Sandra Mansi, taken on July 5, 1977 at a bay on the Vermont side of the lake; the photograph's negative was discarded, and analysts have noted that the bay is only ~14 feet deep, complicating biological interpretations. Both Vermont (1982) and the New York town of Port Henry have passed measures protecting Champ from harm. The creature is one of the most prominent North American lake-monster legends and an important regional cultural and tourism symbol; mainstream scientific consensus regards Champ as a folkloric and misidentification phenomenon rather than a confirmed animal.

etymology.origin: Anglophone shortening of 'Champlain', the lake's name, which itself commemorates French explorer Samuel de Champlain (1567–1635).
etymology.first_use: Popularised in late-19th-century regional press; widespread by the 20th century.

related_phenomena.name: Loch Ness Monster
related_phenomena.description: Scottish lake monster; the prototypical long-necked freshwater cryptid

related_phenomena.name: Memphré
related_phenomena.description: Lake Memphremagog (Vermont/Quebec) lake monster of the same regional folklore complex

features.description: Reports describe a creature with a long, snake-like body, sometimes with humps
Many modern reports — including the Mansi photograph — describe a long, plesiosaur-like neck
Frequent feature of 19th-century newspaper reports and modern lake-monster encounters
Most reports describe dark grey, black, or dark green skin

physical.morphology: Reports are not internally consistent: long-necked plesiosaur-like, eel-like, and 'great serpent' types coexist. No remains or bone have ever been recovered.

abilities.description: Said to spend most of its time submerged, surfacing rarely
A 2003 'Fauna Communications' acoustic survey was claimed to record echolocation-like clicks in the lake; not peer-reviewed and contested

behavior.diet: If real, presumed piscivore (lake fish populations include landlocked salmon, lake trout, perch, gar)
patterns: Reports cluster in summer months when lake recreation peaks
Reports cluster around shallow bays such as Bulwagga Bay

range.description: Lake Champlain, a 125-mile-long freshwater lake forming part of the border between Vermont and New York and extending into the Canadian province of Quebec.

hotspots.name: Bulwagga Bay (Port Henry)

location.description: Shallow bay on the New York side of Lake Champlain near Port Henry; long-running cluster of reports and the site of recent (2024) drone footage

hotspots.notes: Port Henry is host to an annual Champ Day; the town has passed a measure to protect the creature.

hotspots.name: Mansi photograph site (St. Albans Bay area)

location.description: Vermont side of Lake Champlain, north of St. Albans; approximate location reported by Sandra Mansi for her 1977 photograph

hotspots.notes: Mansi later said she could not return to the precise site; the bay is reportedly ~14 feet deep.

first_recorded.source: 'Capt. Crum' Lake Champlain monster newspaper report (1819).

peak_activity_periods.description: Wave of late-19th-century newspaper reports following P. T. Barnum's 1873 reward for the creature's hide
Modern era anchored by the 1977 Mansi photograph and subsequent media attention
Era of acoustic surveys, video recordings, and most recently (2024) drone footage

origins.cultural_roots: Iroquois and Abenaki oral tradition records giant serpents in the lake; the modern English-language 'Champ' tradition develops from 19th-century settler newspaper culture.
origins.earliest_accounts: Iroquois oral tradition; the earliest documented English-language report is 'Capt. Crum' (1819).
origins.folklore_connections: Closely paralleled by Loch Ness Monster traditions and by other North American lake monsters such as Ogopogo (BC), Memphré (Quebec/Vermont), and Bessie (Lake Erie).

timeline.event: Newspaper account of 'Capt. Crum' on Lake Champlain reports a creature estimated at ~187 feet long
timeline.source: 19th-c. American press; cited in Wikipedia and lake-monster surveys

timeline.event: P. T. Barnum offers a reward for Champ's hide
timeline.significance: Triggers a major wave of late-19th-century newspaper reports

timeline.event: Sheriff Nathan H. Mooney reports a serpent-like creature 25–30 feet long in Lake Champlain near Plattsburgh
Sandra Mansi photographs an apparent long-necked creature in Lake Champlain north of St. Albans, Vermont
timeline.significance: Most famous Champ photograph; long called the best lake-monster photograph ever taken
timeline.source: Mansi photograph; Vermont Life and subsequent press

timeline.event: Vermont House of Representatives passes a resolution protecting Champ from harm
timeline.significance: Formal civic protection of the cryptid

timeline.event: Fauna Communications survey claims to record echolocation-like clicks in Lake Champlain
timeline.significance: Acoustic-evidence claim; not peer-reviewed and contested

timeline.event: Bob Aurora and Pete Bodette video apparent large creature in Lake Champlain off Burlington
timeline.significance: Most-discussed video evidence of the 21st century

history.modern_era: Champ is a continuing focus of regional cryptozoology, popular culture, and lake tourism. The 2017–2026 wave of UAP/UAP-adjacent media interest has not produced new physical evidence, but underwater drones, hydrophones, and high-resolution aerial imaging have made fresh, easily shareable encounter footage more common.

notable.name: Sheriff Nathan Mooney sighting

location.description: Lake Champlain near Plattsburgh, New York

notable.description: Sheriff Nathan H. Mooney reported observing a serpent-like creature roughly 25–30 feet long in Lake Champlain, viewed from approximately 110 yards away.

notable.name: Mansi photograph

location.description: Bay on the Vermont side of Lake Champlain, north of St. Albans

notable.description: Sandra Mansi photographed what appears to be a long-necked dark animal partly emerged from Lake Champlain about 150 feet from shore, while on a family outing on the early afternoon of July 5, 1977. The negative was reportedly discarded and the precise location could not later be relocated.
evidence: Original print of the Mansi photograph

credibility.notes: Long described as the best photograph of a lake monster, but with significant provenance gaps.

notable.name: Aurora & Bodette video

location.description: Lake Champlain off Oakledge Park, Burlington, Vermont

types: Two amateur fishermen (Bob Aurora and Pete Bodette)

notable.description: Two fishermen recorded several minutes of video of an apparent large undulating creature in Lake Champlain off Burlington. The footage was reviewed on national television and discussed by FBI and Coast Guard analysts as ambiguous.

credibility.notes: Most-discussed Champ video of the 21st century.

photographic.name: Mansi photograph
photographic.description: Single colour photograph by Sandra Mansi of an apparent long-necked dark animal in Lake Champlain.
photographic.analysis: Long described as the best lake-monster photograph; the negative was discarded and the location could not later be re-identified. The bay where it was reportedly taken is shallow.

video.name: Aurora–Bodette video
video.description: Camcorder footage of an apparent large creature off Burlington, Vermont.
video.analysis: Aired on ABC News; FBI and Coast Guard analysts interviewed by ABC declined to identify a known animal, but the video is too ambiguous for conclusive analysis.

audio.name: Fauna Communications acoustic survey
audio.description: Hydrophone recordings claimed to contain echolocation-like clicks; reported by Fauna Communications Research Institute.
audio.analysis: Not peer-reviewed; explanations including known fish vocalisations have been proposed.

scientific.name: Relict population of unknown large aquatic animal
scientific.description: Hypothesis that Champ represents a small population of an unknown or relict large aquatic animal — variously suggested as a long-necked plesiosaur-like reptile or a giant eel — surviving in Lake Champlain.

scientific.name: Misidentified known species
scientific.description: Champ sightings are best explained by misidentified known animals: lake sturgeon (which can exceed 7 feet), garfish, otters in line, or floating logs and wave-trains.
evidence_cited: Recurrent identification of long-necked 'monsters' as otter chains in many lakes

skeptical.name: Cultural / tourism-driven legend
skeptical.description: Champ's modern profile is closely tied to regional tourism; the legend has been actively promoted by local government and the Vermont Lake Monsters baseball team, which uses Champ as its mascot.
evidence_cited: Spike in reports following P. T. Barnum's 1873 reward and again following 1981 Vermont Life Mansi article

traditions: Iroquois and Abenaki oral traditions of great water-serpents
Vermont and upstate New York lake-monster folklore
stories: P. T. Barnum's 1873 reward for the creature's hide
folklore.beliefs: Local tradition treats Champ as a real, if elusive, animal of the lake; protection ordinances reflect both genuine belief and tourism-friendly civic identity.

indigenous.significance: The Mohawk Onyare'kowa ('great horned serpent') tradition predates the colonial 'Champ' label and forms part of a wider Iroquoian and Algonquian inheritance of powerful water-beings.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: Indigenous water-serpent traditions should not be conflated with the modern cryptozoological 'Champ' label.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Cite Mohawk and Abenaki sources directly when referencing pre-contact tradition.
